//: SFAF Calendar - committed Claude Code permissions.
GOAL: routine work runs without interruption; irreversible work stops and asks.
WHY THE ASK LIST EXISTS, AND WHY IT SHOULD NOT BE WIDENED CASUALLY.
Earlier in this project a working transcript containing a live credential was
force-pushed to GitHub. It was recoverable for exactly one reason: somebody was
asked before it happened and stopped to look. Every entry in permissions.ask
buys back that pause. None of it blocks anything - answering yes is a single
keystroke. The cost of a false positive is one second; the cost of a false
negative is a credential in a public repository. Weigh accordingly before
deleting an entry, and note that an entry which has never fired is an entry
doing its job, not a dead one.
PATH SYNTAX ON THIS MACHINE, BECAUSE IT IS NOT WHAT YOU WOULD GUESS.
Claude Code on Windows here writes absolute path rules in POSIX form with the
drive as a lowercase segment behind a double slash:
Read(//c/Users/msapoznikov/Documents/Apps/**)
NOT C:\Users\... and NOT /c/Users/... . A rule in the wrong form matches
nothing and fails silently, which looks exactly like a rule that is working.
This file therefore avoids absolute paths entirely: the file tools are allowed
as bare tool-name rules, which cannot mis-glob, and Claude Code already confines
them to the project directory. If you ever do add an absolute rule, copy the
shape above rather than inventing one, and check it against .claude/
settings.local.json, which is written by the harness itself and is the only
reliable source of truth for the format.
TWO LAYERS, ON PURPOSE.
permissions.ask below is the portable first line and needs no shell. But its
Bash patterns are globs anchored at the front of the command, so they cannot
catch a flag that moves: 'git push --force' is matched, 'git push origin
--force' is not. The PreToolUse hook closes that gap by regex-matching the
whole command string, and it was verified against 18 destructive spellings and
25 routine ones before being committed. Keep both. The rules survive a machine
with no bash; the hook survives an argument order nobody anticipated.
settings.local.json is gitignored. Personal 'always allow' clicks land there
and must not accumulate into this file, which is meant to be read and reasoned
about rather than grown by reflex.
AUDITED 2026-08-06, ON EVIDENCE FROM ELEVEN SESSIONS.
settings.local.json had grown to 252 unreviewed allow rules. 220 were already
covered by this file and could grant nothing; 3 overlapped rules this file
deliberately asks about, one of them git filter-repo; the rest were one-off
command strings, several pointing at scratch directories that no longer exist.
It is now three WebFetch domains.
The categories that were genuinely missing from THIS file, and were the reason
the local one kept growing, have been added: php (the language this plugin is
written in, linted before every build), bash .claude/* (the two scripts that
exist to be run), xargs, and three read-only git subcommands. The rule is that
anything worth allowing twice is a category and belongs here.
The guard hook has a test now: bash .claude/guard-test.sh. It was run against
17 destructive spellings and 18 routine ones, all passing. The hook has never
fired in any recorded session, and never firing is the intended steady state -
but a guard nobody has tested is a guard nobody knows the shape of, which is
the exact failure this file warns about two paragraphs up.
